title: Your first script
summary: Put commands in a file, make it runnable, give it arguments, and start from a template that checks them.

text: A script is a text file of commands, run from top to bottom. It runs later, without you watching: that changes how you write it.
- The first line, #! (the shebang), says which program reads the file.
- env finds bash in your PATH. On a Mac, /bin/bash is an old 3.2; the bash you install (brew install bash) is newer, and env picks it.

scheme: "$@"  all of them, each one whole
text: - chmod +x makes the file runnable, and ./ runs the one in this folder.
- $1, $2… are the arguments. "$@", with its quotes, hands them all on, and a name with a space stays one argument.
Every script fight starts from this shape, a template:
- die writes an error on stderr (>&2) and stops with a non-zero status, so whoever ran the script, a person or cron, knows it failed.
- main checks its arguments first, then does the work. The last line hands it the script's arguments.

scheme: $ bash -x lines.sh f     each line as it runs
text: - bash -n checks the syntax and runs nothing. bash -x shows each line with its values: the way to see where a script goes wrong.
- ShellCheck (install it with apt, dnf or brew) reads a script and names the traps of the next lessons, each with a page that explains it.
